analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards for pain and suffering in medical malpractice cases and shields drug makers from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The bill received no committee hearing or vote after being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2011, and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for medical malpractice and medical-product lawsuits nationwide. It caps compensation for pain, suffering, and disfigurement at $250,000 no matter how many defendants are liable, caps lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale, and lets juries hear that the injured person had insurance. It makes punitive damages — the extra penalty meant to punish reckless conduct — available only for intentional or malicious harm, and bars them entirely against drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA. Actual out-of-pocket losses like medical bills and lost wages would remain fully recoverable.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care providers facing malpractice insurance premiums, the insurers who write those policies, and pharmaceutical and device manufacturers, who would face lower damage exposure, stricter standards for punitive awards, and near-total immunity from punitive damages for FDA-approved products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Physicians, hospitals, liability insurers, drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages — compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life — at $250,000 per injury, regardless of how many parties are sued or how many claims are brought [S3].
Keeps economic damages (medical bills, lost earnings) fully recoverable without a cap [S3].
Caps lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale: 40% of the first $50,000, down to 15% of anything above $600,000 [S3].

Allows punitive damages only when the defendant acted with intent to injure or deliberately ignored certain harm, proven by clear and convincing evidence, and caps them at the greater of two times economic damages or $250,000 [S3].

Prohibits punitive damages against manufacturers, distributors, and suppliers of any medical product approved, cleared, or licensed by the FDA — with an exception only if the company misrepresented or withheld required information from the FDA or bribed an FDA official [S3].
Prevents insurers and other benefit providers from recouping or placing liens on a patient's award, so the injured person keeps more of what is recovered [S3].
Allows courts to order future damage awards of $50,000 or more to be paid in periodic installments rather than as a lump sum [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Injured patients whose largest losses are not financial: children, retirees, stay-at-home parents, and people with modest earnings whose harm is mostly pain, disfigurement, or loss of enjoyment of life, since the $250,000 cap applies no matter how severe the injury. The broader cost is weaker deterrence against negligent care, since careless providers face less financial exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured patients with large non-financial losses

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap falls hardest on patients whose injuries are catastrophic but whose monetary losses are small — a child, a retiree, or a parent who stays home — because pain and suffering is often the largest component of what a severe injury is worth [S3].
The bill lets juries hear that the injured person had health insurance, which can push awards down even though the patient (or taxpayers) paid premiums for that coverage [S3].

Barring punitive damages for FDA-approved products leaves patients without a financial penalty tool against manufacturers even for conduct short of deliberately lying to the FDA, effectively treating federal approval as conclusive proof of safety [S3].
A one-year deadline after discovering an injury (with a hard three-year outer limit and limited exceptions) can be too short for injuries that reveal themselves slowly [S3].

The stated purpose of lowering malpractice premiums and reducing 'defensive medicine' is asserted in the bill's findings but is not guaranteed by its terms; the caps reduce payments to injured patients with certainty, while any savings for the health system depend on insurers and providers passing them along [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give doctors, hospitals, and drug makers a large and certain reduction in legal exposure, while the promised benefits for patients — lower costs, better access — rest on the contested claim that malpractice suits drive up health spending. The costs fall with certainty on the small number of patients with the worst injuries, and the caps are not tied to any requirement that insurers lower premiums or that providers pass savings on. It is a straightforward transfer of risk and cost from the medical and insurance industries to injured patients, with the size of the benefit to the public genuinely uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Roy Blunt introduced S. 1099 on May 26, 2011, on behalf of himself and Sen. Mark Kirk [S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary — the only action it ever received [S5].
It drew just 2 cosponsors, both Republicans [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded for the bill, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, injured patients kept the existing state-law rules on malpractice compensation, and the medical and insurance industries avoided a federal cap on damages but gained nothing either.

for.name: Sen. Mark Kirk
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer when it was introduced

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; every supporter in the record was a Republican, but the bill died for lack of committee action, not an opposing vote.

industries.note: Caps on jury awards and stricter punitive-damage standards would directly limit what insurers pay out on malpractice claims. The savings flow to insurers and providers only if premiums are reduced; the cost falls on injured patients.

The bill bars punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved products, so a manufacturer whose drug passes FDA review could not be hit with a punitive award for harm short of deliberately lying to the agency. Patients hurt by such products would have weaker financial recourse.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers would face a $250,000 ceiling on pain-and-suffering awards, a shield from punitive damages, and protection from being named in product-liability suits for dispensing FDA-approved drugs. The trade-off for patients is less compensation and less financial deterrence against negligent care.

Sliding-scale fee caps and a longer list of admissible defenses would reduce what malpractice attorneys can recover, which dampens the private financial incentive to bring injured patients' cases. Their interest in this bill runs with patients' interests.

industries.industry: Health and disability insurers and government benefit programs
industries.note: Juries could hear that an injured patient had insurance, tending to lower awards, but the bill also forbids these payers from placing liens on or recovering from the patient's award, which would cost them subrogation revenue.
